title.text: Classification: predicting a yes or no answer with logistic regression and a decision tree

objects.text: How do we predict a category, and what does the model's confidence mean?

AI and Data Science Professional  |  Session 15 of 24  |  Module D: Machine learning
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome back. Last session you built a first model for loan default and compared it with the laziest guesser we can build. Today the question is sharper. How confident is the model, and what do we do with that confidence?

You will fit two kinds of model on the Nile Microfinance loans, learn to read what they say, and choose a decision threshold using the cost of a mistake. That last step is the one a manager cares about.

slides.notes:
Here is what you can do by the end of today. You can say what binary classification is, and you can fit two models on the Nile Microfinance loans: a logistic regression and a decision tree. You can read the predicted probability each model gives, and you can turn text variables such as occupation into numbers a model can use.

And you can choose a decision threshold from the cost of a missed default and the cost of a false alarm. That last part is where data science meets a manager's budget.

Your two hours: concepts first,
then a Python lab in Colab

slides.notes:
We have two hours. The first ten minutes bring back Session 14 and set the question for today. Then forty-five minutes of concepts, with no laptops open, so you can watch the pictures and follow the worked examples. After a ten minute break you open the Colab notebook for a forty-five minute lab.

You will predict each answer, run the cell, read the output, and then change one thing. The last ten minutes are an exit check and what you keep. The lab is where the learning sticks, so please protect that time.

runs.text: 1.  In the loan file, which variables are the features and which is the target?

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 14. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. In the loan file, which variables are the features and which is the target?

A good answer is this. The features are the inputs, such as income, loan amount and age. The target is default: 1 means the loan defaulted, 0 means it was repaid.

Question two. Why do we hide a test set from the model?

A good answer is this. To score the model on loans it has never seen, like a test with new questions. A score on the training set flatters the model.

Question three. What is a baseline model, and why do we compare against one?

A good answer is this. The simplest possible model. Here it says "no default" for every loan and is right 87.45 percent of the time (1,749 of the 2,000 test loans). Any model we build must beat it.

If you missed one, check your notes from last session tonight. Now to today.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: Predicting one of two categories. The positive class is the outcome we look for: default = 1. The negative class is the other: repaid = 0.
A model that bends a score from the features into a probability between 0 and 1 with the sigmoid. scikit-learn penalises large coefficients (regularisation, C = 1.0).
A model made of yes or no questions. Each path ends in a leaf node, and the leaf gives the predicted probability.
The probability at or above which we predict the positive class. The default of 0.5 is rarely right for a business.
Turning a text variable into one 0 or 1 indicator column per category, so a model can use it.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Binary classification (positive class, negative class). Predicting one of two categories. The positive class is the outcome we look for: default = 1. The negative class is the other: repaid = 0.

Logistic regression (sigmoid, log-odds, regularisation). A model that bends a score from the features into a probability between 0 and 1 with the sigmoid. scikit-learn penalises large coefficients (regularisation, C = 1.0).

Decision tree (root node, leaf node). A model made of yes or no questions. Each path ends in a leaf node, and the leaf gives the predicted probability.

Decision threshold (cut-off). The probability at or above which we predict the positive class. The default of 0.5 is rarely right for a business.

One-hot encoding. Turning a text variable into one 0 or 1 indicator column per category, so a model can use it.

title.text:
Binary classification predicts one
of two categories for each loan

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsh_target_7.70x4.80_1b46ccd4.png
objects.alt: Binary classification predicts one of two categories for each loan

objects.text: Classification predicts a category. Binary classification has exactly two.

runs.text: Positive class: the outcome we look for. Here default = 1.
Negative class: the other outcome. Here repaid, default = 0.
In Excel: a Yes or No column to fill in for new loans.

slides.notes:
A few real rows from the Nile Microfinance loans file. Every column on the left is a feature, an input we know when the loan is approved. The gold column is the target, also called the label. Predicting a category is called classification, and when there are exactly two categories it is binary classification.

One category is the positive class, the outcome we look for, which here is a default and is coded one. The other is the negative class, a repaid loan, coded zero. Positive does not mean good. It means the one we are hunting. In Excel this is a Yes or No column you wish you could fill in.

Which class is the positive class in your own work?

You already know every idea of today from Excel, so here is the translation. A Yes or No column is the target, or label. A percentage beside each row is the predicted probability. The number in an IF formula that decides yes or no is the decision threshold, also called the classification threshold or cut-off.

A helper column for each category is one-hot encoding. A trendline that returns a probability is logistic regression, and a nested IF written by the computer is a decision tree. When you read documentation or a job advert, this table is your dictionary. Which of these words was new to you?

title.text:
Only 12.6 percent of loans default,
so the positive class is rare

objects.text: 1,004 of the 8,000 loans defaulted. About one loan in eight is in the positive class.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_waffle_4.40x4.30_94365bd6.png
objects.alt: Only 12.6 percent of loans default, so the positive class is rare

slides.notes:
Before any model, look at how common the positive class is. In the Nile Microfinance file, the same 8,000 loans as in Session 14, 1,004 loans defaulted. That is 12.6 percent, about one loan in eight, so roughly thirteen in every hundred squares on the picture. When one class is much rarer than the other, we call it class imbalance.

It is the reason a model can look good and still be useless, and it shapes every choice today and next session. Why is a rare positive class harder to predict?

title.text:
Default rate climbs with the
instalment-to-income ratio

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_bars_11.90x4.25_1ad0d265.png
objects.alt: Default rate climbs with the instalment-to-income ratio

objects.text: Five equal groups of 1,600 loans. The 1.15 in the ratio is assumed.

slides.notes:
In Session 14 we built a feature called instalment to income, the instalment-to-income ratio: the monthly instalment divided by the monthly income, where the instalment is the loan plus a fifteen percent charge, spread over the term. That fifteen percent is an illustrative assumption. A ratio of one means the instalment equals a whole month of income.

Here the loans are cut into five equal groups by the ratio. In the lightest fifth, 4.8 percent defaulted. In the heaviest fifth, 31.7 percent defaulted, about 7 times as many. A classification model has to find a pattern like this one. Which loan in your portfolio would you call heavy?

title.text:
Occupation is text, yet it
carries a signal a model can use

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_bars_11.90x4.25_454c9a6a.png
objects.alt: Occupation is text, yet it carries a signal a model can use

objects.text: Share of loans that defaulted in each occupation. A model needs these words as numbers.

slides.notes:
Now a text variable. Occupation has seven values. Boda rider borrowers defaulted most, at 19.8 percent, about one loan in five. Teachers defaulted least, at 8.0 percent. The five jobs in between sit from 11.0 to 14.2 percent. So occupation carries some information. But a model works on numbers, and a word like Teacher is not a number.

In a few slides you will see how one-hot encoding fixes that. Would you expect occupation to matter in your own lending data?

title.text:
A straight line can leave the range 0 to 1, so
logistic regression bends it with the sigmoid

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsh_sigmoid_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: A straight line can leave the range 0 to 1, so logistic regression bends it with the sigmoid

objects.text: A probability must stay between 0 and 1. A straight line does not.

runs.text: The sigmoid (logistic) function squeezes any score into 0 to 1.
Logistic regression: a linear score, then the sigmoid.
Despite the word regression, it is a classification model.

slides.notes:
Why not use plain linear regression for a yes or no answer?

Look at the red dashed line. A straight line keeps going: it would predict minus point two for one loan and one point four for another, and neither is a probability. The black curve is the sigmoid, also called the logistic function. It takes any score, however large or small, and squeezes it into a number between zero and one.

At a score of zero the probability is exactly point five. Logistic regression is a linear score followed by this curve. The word regression is historical. It is a classification model. What would a probability of one point four mean to a credit manager?

title.text:
Logistic regression: a linear score z
becomes a probability p by the sigmoid

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_math_11.90x1.83_e974fc5a.png
objects.alt: Logistic regression: a linear score z becomes a probability p by the sigmoid

rows.text: The score, also the log-odds ln(p / (1 - p))
Predicted probability of default. In Excel: =1/(1+EXP(-z))
Intercept: the score when every feature is 0
One coefficient per feature (per 1 standard deviation), learned from the training set
The feature values of one loan, standardised (z-scores)

slides.notes:
Here is the whole model in three lines. First, a score z: an intercept plus each feature times its coefficient, exactly like the line you know from regression. Second, the probability p is one divided by one plus e to the power minus z. In Excel that is one divided by one plus EXP of minus z.

Third, the same relationship read backwards: z is the log-odds, the natural log of p over one minus p. The coefficients are learned from the training loans, after a StandardScaler has put every variable on the same scale. Each symbol is named in the table with a value from one real test loan, which we work through in a moment.

Which part of this is already familiar from Session 13?

title.text:
Log-odds is another way to write
a probability: 0 means even odds

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_coin_0.39.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_coin_0.39.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_coin_0.39.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_check_0.39.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_chart_0.39.png

objects.text: Odds are what bookmakers quote. A positive log-odds means the positive class is more likely than not.

slides.notes:
Probability, odds and log-odds are three ways to say the same thing. Odds are p divided by one minus p. A probability of point two is odds of point two five, which is one to four against. The log-odds is the natural log of the odds. At probability point five the odds are even and the log-odds is zero.

Below point five the log-odds is negative, above it positive. A probability of 0.10 has log-odds -2.20. Why bother?

Because the log-odds can take any value, so a linear score can model it freely, and the sigmoid converts it back. Can you read the table from probability to log-odds in one row?

title.text:
One loan, step by step: from
features to a predicted probability

objects.text: Loan N04300 from the test set: Boda rider, instalment-to-income ratio 0.79, late payments 0.
1 Score z
Intercept -2.23, ratio +0.65, late payments -0.17, Boda rider +0.41, 24 other terms +0.22. Sum z = -1.12.
2 Probability
p = 1 / (1 + e^1.12) = 0.25: a 25 percent chance of default.
3 Decision
At threshold 0.20 the loan is flagged. At 0.50 it is not.
4 Reality
In the data this loan defaulted. One loan proves nothing: we judge all 2,000 test loans.

slides.notes:
Let us follow one loan from the test set through the model. Step one, the score. The intercept is -2.23. The ratio term adds 0.65, because the instalment-to-income ratio is the strongest predictor. Each term is a coefficient times the loan's standardised value. The late payments term adds -0.17, the occupation term adds 0.41, and the other twenty four terms together add 0.22.

The score z is -1.12. Step two, the sigmoid turns that into a probability of 0.25. Step three, at a threshold of point two the loan is flagged. In the data this loan defaulted, but one loan proves nothing. Which step would you check first if the probability looked wrong?

title.text:
A coefficient shows the direction of an effect, and its
exponent shows the change in odds per standard deviation

rows.text: Per standard deviation (about 0.44): odds multiplied by this much.
Each late-payment step raises the odds.
Higher odds than the other occupations.
Lower odds than the other occupations.

objects.text: Per 1 standard deviation, other features fixed. scikit-learn adds a penalty by default (regularisation, C = 1.0), so a different scaling or C changes them.

slides.notes:
After fitting, the model is a list of coefficients, and we can read them. A positive coefficient raises the log-odds of default, a negative one lowers it. Raise e to the power of the coefficient and you get the odds ratio: the factor by which the odds of default are multiplied when that feature rises by one standard deviation, holding the others fixed.

The instalment-to-income ratio has a coefficient of 0.80, an odds ratio of 2.23. Boda rider has an odds ratio of 1.14 and teacher 0.98. Be careful: scikit-learn also applies a penalty on large coefficients by default, called regularisation, with C equal to one, so the sizes depend on the scaling.

What does an odds ratio below one tell you?

title.text:
One-hot encoding turns each occupation
into its own column of 0 and 1

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsh_onehot_11.90x4.25_52ab325c.png
objects.alt: One-hot encoding turns each occupation into its own column of 0 and 1

objects.text: get_dummies makes 15 indicator columns from 3 text variables: 12 columns become 27.

slides.notes:
Models need numbers, so a text variable must be encoded. One-hot encoding makes one new column for each category. A record gets a one in the column of its own category and zero in all the others, and only one column is hot. On the slide, a mechanic gets a one in the Mechanic column.

In our loans file, three text variables, gender, occupation and loan purpose, became fifteen indicator columns, so twelve numeric columns became 27. In regression in statistics software you drop one level to avoid the dummy variable trap, where one column can be predicted exactly from the others. Scikit-learn's logistic regression penalises large coefficients, called regularisation, so it copes with all of them.

Why can we not simply number the occupations from 1 to 7?

title.text:
A decision tree (depth 2) asks yes or no questions,
and each leaf gives a predicted probability

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsh_tree_11.90x4.25_da106181.png
objects.alt: A decision tree (depth 2) asks yes or no questions, and each leaf gives a predicted probability

objects.text: Depth 2 (the lab tree has one more level), 6,000 training loans. Gold leaf: 25 percent or more default.

slides.notes:
This tree was fitted on the 6,000 training loans. The top question asks whether the instalment to income ratio is at most 0.75. Of all the loans, 12.6 percent defaulted. Loans that answer yes go left, where the default rate is 8.3 percent, and loans that answer no go right, where it is 38.6 percent.

Each side asks a second question. At the bottom are the leaves, and each leaf gives a probability: the share of training loans in that leaf that defaulted. Follow any loan from the top and you reach exactly one leaf. Which leaf would you worry about?

title.text:
A tree has a root node, internal
nodes and leaf nodes joined by splits

rows.text: The first question, asked of every training loan.
One question on one feature with a threshold. The yes and no answers send loans down two branches.
A question asked after the first one.
An end point with no further question. Its predicted probability is the share of its training loans that defaulted.
The most questions on any path from root to leaf. We set max_depth to stop the tree growing without limit.

slides.notes:
Here is the vocabulary of trees, with the tree you will fit in the lab, which is three questions deep. The root node is the first question, here instalment_to_income <= 0.75, asked of all 6,000 training loans. A split is one question on one feature with a threshold.

An internal node is a question asked after the first one. A leaf node is an end point: no more questions, and its probability is the share of training loans that defaulted there. Depth is the longest path of questions. We limit it with max depth, because an unlimited tree memorises the training loans.

How many leaves can a tree of depth three have at most?

title.text:
A tree chooses each split to make the two
groups purer, measured by Gini impurity

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_math_11.90x2.33_3c88797c.png
objects.alt: A tree chooses each split to make the two groups purer, measured by Gini impurity

rows.text: Impurity: 0 is pure, 0.5 is an even mix
Share of the group in class k
Loans sent left and right by the split
Weighted average of the two groups: the lowest wins

slides.notes:
How does the tree choose its questions?

It measures how mixed a group is, using Gini impurity. If a group is all one class the impurity is zero. If it is an even mix it is point five. At the root, 12.6 percent of the training loans defaulted, which gives an impurity of 0.219. The tree then tries every feature and every threshold.

For each candidate it computes the impurity of the two groups, weighted by their size. The split instalment_to_income <= 0.75 gives 0.197, the lowest, so it becomes the root. Then the tree repeats the search inside each group. The weights are the group sizes, so a tiny pure group cannot hide a large mixed one.

Scikit-learn's default criterion is called gini. Why do you think the tree must try every threshold?

If you have ever written a nested IF in Excel, you have written a tiny decision tree. On the left, you decide the questions and the thresholds from experience. On the right, the computer searches the training loans for the questions and thresholds that best separate the defaulted loans from the repaid ones.

The output has the same shape: a path of yes or no answers that ends in a verdict. The tree gives a probability at the end. The rule on the left, with the ratio above one point five, is only an illustration I made up. The first question the tree found is instalment_to_income <= 0.75.

Which kind of rule would your loan officers write?

slides.notes:
This picture shows the logistic regression's predicted probabilities on the 2,000 test loans, as a share of each group in each bin. White bars are repaid loans, gold bars are defaulted loans. Defaulted loans tend to sit further to the right, so the model has learned something. But the groups overlap, so no decision threshold is perfect.

The red line is a decision threshold of point two. At that threshold 43 percent of the defaulted loans are flagged, and also 10 percent of the repaid loans. The function predict in scikit-learn uses point five without telling you. Where would you put the line?

title.text:
Moving the decision threshold trades
missed defaults for false alarms

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_lock_0.39.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_bell_0.39.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_bell_0.39.png

objects.text: Logistic regression on the 2,000 test loans, of which 251 defaulted. For reading only: we do not pick a threshold from this table. TP, FP, FN: true positive, false positive, false negative.

slides.notes:
Now we move the threshold and count what happens on the 2,000 test loans, 251 of which defaulted. At the usual point five, the model flags only 67 loans. It catches 51 defaults and misses 200. Lower the threshold to point two and it flags 278 loans, catching 108 and missing 143, but it raises 170 false alarms.

At point one it catches 175 and raises 619 false alarms. A false alarm is a false positive and a missed default is a false negative. No threshold wins on both. We read this table to see the trade-off. We do not pick the threshold from it, because the test loans must stay unseen until the end.

So how do we choose?

title.text:
The two mistakes cost different amounts,
so the threshold is a business decision

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_cross_0.75.png

objects.text: A missed default

runs.text: A false negative: the loan is not repaid.
Illustrative cost: UGX 1,000,000, the principal lost.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_bell_0.75.png

objects.text: A false alarm

runs.text: A false positive: a good borrower is refused.
Illustrative cost: UGX 100,000, the interest not earned.

objects.text: These two costs are teaching numbers. Use your own lender's.

slides.notes:
The threshold is a business decision, because the two mistakes cost different amounts. A missed default is a false negative: the money goes out and does not come back. For teaching we say that costs one million shillings. In our file the average defaulted loan is about 1,829,000 shillings, so the order of magnitude is realistic, but these costs are illustrative.

A false alarm is a false positive: a good borrower is refused and the lender loses the interest, which we set at one hundred thousand shillings, also illustrative. A real lender would use its own figures. Which mistake does your organisation fear more?

title.text:
Cross-validation on the training loans finds a
threshold of 0.10, close to the cost rule 0.0909

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dsh_curve_11.90x4.25_37516f9b.png
objects.alt: Cross-validation on the training loans finds a threshold of 0.10, close to the cost rule 0.0909

objects.text: Training loans, 5-fold. Illustrative: UGX 1,000,000 per missed default, UGX 100,000 per false alarm.

slides.notes:
The threshold must be chosen without looking at the test loans. So we use only the 6,000 training loans. Cross-validation splits them into five parts. Each part gets probabilities from a model trained on the other four. Then we price the mistakes at every threshold, scaled to 2,000 loans.

It is lowest at 0.10, where it is 136 million, against 209 million at point five. The dashed lines are the extremes. There is also a handy rule that needs no data. If the probabilities are well calibrated, flag a loan when p is at least the cost of a false alarm divided by the sum of both costs, which is 100,000 over 1,100,000, or 0.0909.

The curve is flat from 0.08 to 0.12, so both answers are as good. What would change if a false alarm cost five hundred thousand?

the cost of the choices already made

objects.text: Illustrative costs, 2,000 test loans, 251 defaults. Searching the test loans would find 0.08 at UGX 133.1 million, a gain of under UGX 5 million that exists only on these loans. We do not do that.

slides.notes:
Now, and only now, we use the test loans, once. The default threshold of point five costs 201.6 million shillings. The threshold from cross-validation, 0.10, costs 137.9 million: it flags 794 loans, catches 175 of the 251 defaults, and raises 619 false alarms. The cost rule, 0.0909, costs 133.9 million.

Flagging nobody costs 251.0 million and flagging everybody 174.9 million. Someone could ask: why not search the test loans for the cheapest threshold?

It would give 0.08 and 133.1 million, a saving of under five million that exists only on these two thousand loans. That is tuning on the test set, and the score would be optimistic. Which of the two honest choices would you present to your manager?

title.text:
Read the recipe before the lab:
six lines fit and use both models

runs.text: X = pd.get_dummies(features, dtype=int)
model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_prob = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(
max_depth=3, random_state=42)

objects.text: In plain words

runs.text: Line 1: one-hot encode the text. 12 numeric columns become 27.
Lines 2 and 3: a StandardScaler, then logistic regression with its defaults (L2 penalty, C = 1.0).
Line 4: fit on the training loans.
Line 5: column 1 of predict_proba is the probability of default.
Lines 6 and 7: a tree with at most three questions.

slides.notes:
Before the lab, read the recipe. Line one, get dummies, does the one-hot encoding, and twelve numeric columns become 27. Lines two and three build a pipeline: a standard scaler puts every variable on the same scale, then the logistic regression runs with its defaults, an L2 penalty and C equal to one, called regularisation.

That is why the coefficients depend on the scaling. Line four fits on the training loans, which you split in Session 14: 6,000 to learn from and 2,000 kept hidden. Line five asks for probabilities. Predict proba returns two columns, and column one is the probability of default, the positive class.

Lines six and seven create a tree with at most three questions. To flag loans you then compare y prob with a decision threshold. Which line would you change to try a different threshold?

title.text: Five likely mistakes in the lab and how to fix them

rows.text: ValueError: could not convert string to float
A text variable such as occupation is still in X.
Run pd.get_dummies on the features before fitting.
A misspelt or already dropped column.
Print df.columns and copy the exact name.
A probability above 0.9 for many loans
You used the leaking column collection_calls.
predict_proba gives two columns and the numbers look backwards
Column 0 is the probability of repaid.
Take column 1 for the probability of default.
ValueError: Found input variables with inconsistent numbers of samples
X and y have different row counts, for example one was filtered and the other not.
Filter both, or filter before you split.

Five messages you may meet. A ValueError about converting a string to a float means a text variable is still in your features, so run get dummies first. A KeyError means a misspelt column name, so print the columns and copy the name. Probabilities above point nine for many loans mean you kept the collection calls column.

Drop it, and we explain why next session. If the numbers look backwards, you probably took column zero of predict proba, which is the probability of repaid. Last, a ValueError about inconsistent numbers of samples means X and y have different row counts, so filter both together. Read the message first. It usually tells you the answer.

title.text:
Exit check: three questions, then
compare with the short answers

rows.text: A model gives a loan p = 0.30. What does that number mean, and what does a threshold of 0.20 do with it?
A 30 percent chance of default, as the model estimates. At threshold 0.20 the loan is flagged, because 0.30 is at or above 0.20.
Why do we one-hot encode occupation before fitting?
The model works on numbers. One-hot encoding gives each occupation its own 0 or 1 column, with no false order between them.
A missed default costs ten times a false alarm. Should the threshold be higher or lower than 0.50, and why?
Lower. Missing a default is the dearer mistake, so flag more loans and accept more false alarms.
